title: Pharmacies and medicines in Mauritius
summary: How pharmacies are licensed and who regulates them, when you need a prescription and what it must contain, what a pharmacist owes you, how medicine prices are controlled, what the public health service provides at no charge, and where to complain. Checked on 20 November 2026.
audience: Residents, newcomers and visitors who need a medicine and want to know the rules before they reach the counter.

facts.label: Where medicines may be sold
facts.detail: Pharmacy Act, section 17. A doctor may sell medicines only where there is no pharmacy within 5 kilometres.

facts.label: Who licenses a pharmacy
facts.detail: The licence is valid for one year. Every pharmacy must have a pharmacist in charge.

facts.label: Community pharmacies
facts.detail: With 45 wholesale pharmacies. The Ministry's figure, on an undated page.

facts.label: Registered pharmacists
facts.detail: Registered with the Pharmacy Council of Mauritius. Same undated page.

facts.label: Who may write a prescription
facts.value: A medical practitioner, a dental surgeon or a veterinary surgeon
facts.detail: The Act calls them authorised persons.

facts.label: Antibiotics
facts.value: Sold by retail on prescription only
facts.detail: Pharmacy Act, section 32, on therapeutic substances.

facts.label: Prescription for a dangerous drug
facts.value: Must be presented within 7 days of its date
facts.detail: Dangerous Drugs Act 2000, section 19. It can be dispensed once only.

facts.label: Public health service
facts.detail: Around 73% of the population uses it, the Ministry says.

facts.label: Price at the counter
facts.value: Not above the retail price affixed to the product
facts.detail: Code of Practice for Pharmacists. Mark-ups on pharmaceutical products are capped.

facts.label: Ambulance
facts.detail: The SAMU control room answers 24 hours a day.

sections.heading: How do pharmacies work in Mauritius?

blocks.text: Medicines are sold in pharmacies, and nowhere else. The Pharmacy Act says no person may sell a medicine or drug by retail in any place other than a pharmacy. The one exception is a doctor with no pharmacy within 5 kilometres of the place where the patient is seen. A pharmacy needs a licence from the Pharmacy Board and a pharmacist in charge. The Ministry of Health and Wellness counts 380 community pharmacies across the island and 45 wholesale pharmacies.

You can tell a licensed pharmacy from the outside. The licensee must put up a signboard with his name and the name of the pharmacist in charge, and display the licence inside. The Pharmacy Council tells pharmacists to display their yearly registration certificate for the public to see. A pharmacy may sell only pharmaceutical products, medical and hygiene appliances, toilet preparations and other products that regulations allow.

items: The Pharmacy Board controls the manufacture, importation, distribution and sale of medicines, and grants the licences for retail and wholesale pharmacies. Before granting one it looks at the number of pharmacies in the area and the area's needs. The licence is renewed every year.

The Pharmacy Council of Mauritius, fully in operation since November 2017, regulates the profession. It registers pharmacists, publishes a yearly list of them, sets a Code of Practice and runs disciplinary proceedings. The Ministry gives 555 registered pharmacists.
The Pharmacy Department of the Ministry oversees pharmacy services in the public and private sectors, with 37 Government Pharmacists and 97 Pharmacy Technicians.

blocks.text: For some medicines, yes. The Pharmacy Act forbids selling a therapeutic substance by retail except on a prescription, and it deals with antibiotics under that heading. The same goes for the poisons listed under the Act. Medicines on two of the Act's schedules may be handed over only by a pharmacist, or in the presence of the pharmacist in charge or of an assistant pharmacist.
A prescription is a written order from a medical practitioner, a dental surgeon or a veterinary surgeon. To be valid under the Act it must:

items: be handwritten, dated and signed by the prescriber, and state the prescriber's address;
give the name and address of the patient;
state the total amount to be supplied and the dose to be taken;
carry the words For Dental Treatment Only if a dental surgeon wrote it.

blocks.text: A prescription is dispensed once, unless it says it may be repeated and at what interval. The pharmacy records the date on it and gives you a true copy with a serial number, the date and the pharmacy's stamp. Each medicine's container must carry a label with the instructions for use. A pharmacist may not refuse to dispense a prescription to a person who offers to pay in cash.

sections.heading: What are the rules for dangerous drugs?

blocks.text: They are tighter. Under the Dangerous Drugs Act 2000 a prescription for a dangerous drug must be presented not later than 7 days after its date, and it can be dispensed once only. The pharmacy keeps the original and gives you a stamped copy. A prescriber may not prescribe the drugs in Schedule II of that Act for more than 10 days of treatment, or other Schedule III drugs for more than one month.

sections.heading: What should the pharmacist do for you?

blocks.text: The Code of Practice for Pharmacists, made by regulations in December 2021, binds every registered pharmacist. Among its rules:

items: If the pharmacist thinks the prescriber made an evident error that could endanger you, the law requires him to hold the prescription and check with the prescriber at once.
If the handwriting is unclear, the pharmacist must try to reach the prescriber. If he cannot, he returns the prescription marked handwriting not clear.
Medicines are sold as the entire strip, bearing the expiry date and batch number. Anything sold otherwise is labelled with both.
Where you cannot afford a treatment, the pharmacist substitutes an equivalent generic with your approval and notes it on the prescription. He may also substitute during a shortage.
Products come with a label or a patient leaflet in English or French.
What you tell the pharmacist is confidential, and your privacy is protected during any counselling.

blocks.text: Pharmaceutical products are on the list of goods whose mark-up the Ministry of Commerce and Consumer Protection caps. Most goods on that list have one percentage. Medicines have what the list calls a regressive maximum mark-up. Under the Code of Practice a wholesaler supplies products to pharmacies with a price affixed, and a pharmacist may not sell above that affixed retail price.

sections.heading: Are medicines free in the public health service?

blocks.text: The Ministry says the public health system serves around 73% of the population at no end-user cost, and its Customer Charter lists free access to primary health and hospital care, including specialised treatment, as a main function. Care is given in 5 regional hospitals, 2 district hospitals, specialised hospitals, 19 Area Health Centres, 114 Community Health Centres and 6 Mediclinics, a network meant to put primary care within 3 km of people.

Medicines are dispensed there by Pharmacy Technicians at hospital pharmacies, Area Health Centres, Community Health Centres and Mediclinics. The Ministry's medicines list incorporates the essential medicines recommended by the World Health Organization. In an emergency, call the SAMU ambulance service on 114, which answers 24 hours a day, or go to the Accident and Emergency department of a hospital.

sections.heading: When are pharmacies open at night and on Sundays?

blocks.text: No official source read for this article answers that. The Pharmacy Act sets no opening hours. The Code of Practice only says a pharmacist attends the pharmacy during the hours agreed with its owner. No duty roster published by the Pharmacy Board, the Pharmacy Council or the Ministry was found, so phone the pharmacy before you travel.

items: About a pharmacist's conduct: the Pharmacy Council of Mauritius, 8th Floor, Emmanuel Anquetil Building, Port Louis. Its office is open Monday to Friday from 9 am to 3 pm, on 5912 2664.
About a pharmacy's licence, or a medicine sold outside a pharmacy: the Pharmacy Board, whose reception answers on 490 4200.
About a price above the one marked: the Consumer Affairs Unit of the Ministry of Commerce and Consumer Protection, hotline 185.
About a public hospital or health centre: in person by appointment with the head of the unit, or in writing to the head of the institution or the Regional Health Director.
About a bad reaction to a medicine: tell your pharmacist, who must report adverse drug reactions to the Ministry's Pharmacovigilance Unit.

blocks.text: A breach of the Pharmacy Act is an offence carrying a fine of up to Rs 10,000 and up to 2 years in prison, and a court may cancel or suspend the licence.
